Prohibit

proh-HIB-it -- stress on the second syllable, HIB. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To prohibit is to formally forbid something.

The new city ordinance prohibits parking within twenty feet of every crosswalk.

Worked Example

The librarian points to the sign by the door -- no food, no drinks -- and asks the students to leave their snacks outside.

The library formally forbids food and drink -- that is what it means to prohibit. To prohibit is to ban something by official rule, not merely to frown on it or discourage it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

forbid: to order that something not be done

ban: to officially disallow something

outlaw: to make something illegal

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

permit: to allow something officially

authorize: to give official approval or power for something

Where it sits · how official the ban is — forbid → prohibit → outlaw

forbid vs. prohibit: Forbid is the everyday word and can be purely personal -- a parent forbids dessert before dinner -- while prohibit is formal and official, the language of laws, signs, and regulations.

outlaw vs. prohibit: Outlaw goes beyond prohibit: a prohibited act is banned by a rule, while an outlawed act has been made a crime, placed entirely outside the law.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — pro-

prefix — pro-: before, in front of (Latin)

root — hib- (hab-)

root — hib- (hab-): to hold (Latin habere)

suffix — -it

suffix — -it: a Latin verb ending carried into English (Latin (-itus))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin prohibere combined pro- ('in front of') with habere ('to hold'), and -it is the Latin verb ending carried into English. To prohibit is literally 'to hold something in front' -- blocking an action before it can happen.

Use the root in a new word: inhibit

Use the root in a new word: inhibit: Fear of being laughed at can inhibit even talented students from raising their hands.

Root Check

Word Choice

Prohibit is the formal verb of official rules: laws prohibit littering, and signs announce that smoking is prohibited. It takes either a thing directly ('prohibit fireworks') or 'from' plus an action ('prohibits students from leaving early') -- never 'prohibit to do.'
